title: Learning before breakfast
hookLine: the day begins with a blessing over Torah, then a little study straight away

lines: WHATEVER COMES FIRST SETS THE WEATHER.
cards: A lot of mornings start by taking something in. Headlines. Messages.
Somebody else's photos of somebody else's breakfast. Whatever comes first tends to set the weather for the morning. The Jewish prayer book has an opinion about what should come first.

Very early, before the psalms, before the main prayers, before a single request, there's a blessing for studying Torah. Then, so the blessing isn't left hanging, a few lines to actually study, on the spot.

teach.b: The blessing comes from the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, where several rabbis each offer a wording, and the prayer book keeps more than one.
The first thanks God who commanded us la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah. Not just to read, or to finish, but to be busy with it, the way you're busy with work.
The next asks: make the words of Torah sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children and their children. Sweet, the way honey is sweet.
And the last is the one the Talmud calls the finest of blessings: who chose us and gave us the Torah.

teach.h: THEN A FEW LINES, RIGHT AWAY.
teach.b: Then come a few lines of study, so the blessing has something to bless. In many prayer books, first the priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers, in the old Jewish translation: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee."

teach.h: RECEIVED AS A GIFT, WITH THANKS.
teach.b: Then the lists from yesterday, from the Mishnah and the Talmud. A verse of Torah, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud: a taste of each layer of the tradition. The Talmud takes this blessing seriously.

In tractate Nedarim, it even suggests that when learned people's children didn't become learned, it was because their parents hadn't blessed the Torah first. Study, in this telling, isn't only information.
It's a gift, received with thanks before you open it.

how: Jews who pray each morning say the blessings over the Torah early in the service, then immediately read a few short passages, often the priestly blessing, a mishnah and a passage of Talmud, so the blessing covers the day's study.

games.q: you've just said the blessing over studying Torah. what comes next?
o: move straight on to the psalms.
study a few lines right away.
save the study for the evening.
games.why: the prayer book gives a few lines to study immediately, so the blessing has something to bless: a verse, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud.

practice: Pick up something worth learning from: a page of scripture, a book you trust, even a line from today's lesson.
If you pray, first say la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah; if not, take one breath of thanks for being able to read. Then read one line, slowly, twice.
